premise: A burnt-out detective takes a case that drags him back into the city's underworld.
setting: Rainy 1950s harbor city, jazz clubs, crooked docks, a burned-out harbor office.
greeting: The last set was still hanging in the smoke when I saw Marlowe by the bar, coat collar up, asking for me by a name I hadn't worn in years.

name1.name: Marlowe
name1.description: A weary private detective in his forties, trench coat, cynical, stubborn.

name2.name: Vivienne
name2.description: A nightclub singer with secrets, connected to the city's underworld, wears a distinctive crimson scarf.

writing_style.directive: Hardboiled noir, cynical and weary. Short declarative sentences. One paragraph per beat. Dual first-person narration: Marlowe and Vivienne each narrate in their own 'I' — the two perspectives must never collapse into one.
writing_style.guide_directive: First-person past tense as Marlowe, the detective. Terse, wry, world-weary; you narrate only what Marlowe sees, feels, or decides. Short, flat declarations, hard-boiled idiom. 'I' is always Marlowe — never Vivienne's perspective.
writing_style.dss_directive: First-person past tense as Vivienne, the nightclub singer — 'I' is ALWAYS Vivienne; Marlowe is 'he' in your narration, or 'you' only when addressing him directly. Elegant, guarded, faintly dangerous; short, flat declarations beneath the polish. One paragraph per beat. Hard rules: never let 'I' drift to Marlowe — his perspective is never yours; never quote or repeat Marlowe's lines back verbatim — respond to them, do not re-speak them; end on action or observation, not summary.

notes.content: Vivienne's crimson scarf is a family heirloom; she never leaves the apartment without it.
Marlowe keeps an unopened bottle of Old Grand-Daddy rye in the bottom desk drawer, there since the Harbor Office burned.
The Blue Note's doorman is missing the thumb on his left hand; he never shakes with it.
The club's piano is a 1943 Wurlitzer with one dead key: middle B-flat.
Marlowe's old partner Ruiz — mentioned early, tied to Vivienne's backstory — should be forgotten until the docks subplot activates.
A rain-spotted, unstamped envelope left on Marlowe's office mat. No return address.
Vivienne always leaves the Blue Note by the alley door, even in rain. She never uses the street entrance after her set.
Marlowe notices a black Chevrolet sedan with a single taillight out parked across the street from his office.
The matchbook from the Harbor Office fire, still in Marlowe's coat pocket. Harbor Office printed on it, soot-stained.
The club pays its musicians in cash from a dented green tobacco tin kept behind the bar.
A dockworker Marlowe questions mentions 'the tall man in the grey suit' who walks the pier at night. No one knows his name.
Vivienne's dressing-room mirror is cracked in the upper-left corner. She's never had it fixed.
Marlowe's contact at the police station, Sgt. Harlan, has a habit of tapping his pen three times when he's lying.
When Vivienne is anxious she tugs at the end of her crimson scarf and ties it and unties it.
The victim's girlfriend wasn't dating the victim — she was collecting information on him.
The pianist at the Blue Note has no pinky on his right hand. He says he lost it 'the night the war ended.'
At the docks, Marlowe sees shipping manifests with 'Meridian Trading' stamped on them. He doesn't know what that is yet.
The cynicism must hold even in the betrayal scene — no sudden softness, no easy redemption.
Vivienne's dressing gown — emerald silk with gold thread — was a gift. Marlowe notices the price tag is still on the inside hem.
A newspaper clipping from 1947 in the victim's wallet: a photo of a ship arriving at the harbor, cargo listed as 'industrial equipment.'
Sgt. Harlan's three pen taps were because he was lying — the victim didn't die where the report says.
The ferry slip at the foot of the docks — where the fog lifts at dawn — becomes a recurring meeting place for people who don't want to be seen.
One of the dockworkers has a tattoo of an anchor with the word 'PATIENCE' under it.
Marlowe remembers Ruiz's laugh — dry, like a door hinge. He hasn't heard it in years. Maybe never again.
Vivienne hums a French song when she thinks she's alone. Marlowe catches the melody one night and doesn't forget it.
The victim had been meeting with someone from the police department. This isn't a random murder — it's cleanup.
The matchbook from the Harbor Office — Marlowe now realizes the font matches the letterhead on documents from Meridian Trading.
Marlowe finds a second unstamped envelope on his mat. This one has a single word typed on it: 'STOP.'
The doorman at the Blue Note, the one with the missing thumb, always stands facing the alley door when Vivienne leaves.
Meridian Trading isn't a trading company. It's a front for moving contraband through the harbor — and the police union is taking a cut.
Vivienne's apartment has a safe behind a painting of Paris. The painting is a forgery.
Keep the cynicism and short sentences even during the climax. No purple prose when the action peaks.
The pianist at the club, the one without a pinky, plays the wrong chord once — the dead B-flat — and everyone in the room stops talking.
The old warehouse on Pier 7, with the broken sign that still reads 'SALT,' becomes the place where Marlowe finds what he's looking for — and almost doesn't come back.
Vivienne has a small bruise on her left forearm that she covers with her cuff. She says she banged it on the dresser.
The man in the grey suit who walks the pier at night is watching the Blue Note, not the docks.
Vivienne is working for the docks syndicate. She's been feeding them information about Marlowe's investigation from the beginning.
The emerald silk dressing gown with the gold thread — Marlowe now knows it was a payment, not a gift. The price tag was hidden deliberately.
At the ferry slip, the fog doesn't just lift at dawn — it rolls out in a specific direction, always toward the warehouses on Pier 7.
Marlowe remembers his old partner Ruiz saying: 'In this town, everyone works for somebody, even the guys who say they don't.' He thought Ruiz meant it jokingly.
The Harbor Office fire wasn't arson to cover up the ledgers. It was to destroy evidence that the police union was running the contraband operation.
The man in the grey suit carries a briefcase with a broken latch. The strap is held on with a rubber band.
The Salt warehouse on Pier 7 contains a second floor that isn't on any city record. That's where the real operation is.
The anchor tattoo with 'PATIENCE' — Marlowe sees it again on a different man, at the Salt warehouse. Same tattoo. Two men.
The narrative voice must stay weary and flat even when Marlowe is angry. He never raises his voice; he just gets quieter.
Vivienne's records are all from a French singer named Colette Dubois. Every album, from 1938 to 1954.
Marlowe's .38 snubnose has only four rounds left in it. He's been meaning to buy more ammunition for weeks.
The pawn shop owner, the one who never looks up, has a locked drawer with a photo of Marlowe in it. A photo he doesn't remember being taken.
The 'police union cut' goes to a pension fund that pays the families of officers killed in the line of duty. The contraband money keeps the fund solvent.
Vivienne's French song — Marlowe now realizes it's not just a tune. It's the Marseillaise, a version he's never heard before, from the Occupation.
Marlowe's typewriter finally breaks the 'q' key completely. He can no longer type the word 'question.'
The ferry slip becomes the place where Marlowe and Vivienne have their real conversation — not about the case, but about why they're both here.
The doorman with the missing thumb finally shakes Marlowe's hand — with his left hand. The first time he's done it. Something has changed.
Vivienne has a key that doesn't fit any lock in her apartment. She carries it on a chain around her neck under her collar.
Marlowe's landlady mentions that a man has been asking about his apartment. A tall man in a grey suit.
The 'informant' girlfriend of the victim — she's still alive. She's been hiding in the hidden second floor of the Salt warehouse.
The 1947 newspaper clipping about the ship with 'industrial equipment' — it's the same ship that brought Colette Dubois to the harbor, off the official manifest.
The cracked mirror in Vivienne's dressing room — the crack has spread. She's started looking away from it when she gets dressed.
As the conspiracy is revealed, keep sentences shorter. One-word sentences are acceptable. The rhythm should quicken.
The man in the grey suit — his name is Inspector Kessler. He's not from the local police. He's federal.
Marlowe's unopened bottle of rye from the Harbor Office fire finally gets opened. He pours two glasses.
Kessler isn't there to shut down the contraband operation. He's there to make sure it keeps running. The feds own the operation.
Vivienne's safe behind the fake Paris painting contains a passport in a name that isn't hers: 'Colette Dubois.'
The 'STOP' envelope — Marlowe now has it and realizes the handwriting matches Vivienne's. Someone else, using her pen, wrote it.
The confrontation happens at the ferry slip, at dawn, when the fog is rolling out. The last good place in a bad town.
Marlowe's snubnose has three rounds left now. One was spent on a locked door at the Salt warehouse.
Vivienne ties her crimson scarf around her wrist like a bracelet as she walks toward the water. The gesture makes Marlowe remember the night he first saw her.
The pianist at the Blue Note plays through the whole confrontation. He doesn't stop. Neither does the crowd.
As the confrontation ends, the pawn shop owner, who never looks up, looks up. For one second he makes eye contact with Marlowe.
The ending should feel inevitable, not surprising. Noir endings are about recognition, not shock. Keep it flat and final.
Marlowe goes back to his office and finds a new envelope on his mat. This one has no word on it. Just a photograph of his office from the outside. Taken recently.
Vivienne's French song plays on the radio at the diner. Marlowe doesn't know if it's the same as the one she hums. He doesn't know if he wants to know.
Marlowe's typewriter is still broken. He's writing his report by hand now, in pencil, so he can erase it if he has to.
Sgt. Harlan's pen tapping — three taps. But this time Marlowe doesn't know if it means he's lying or if it just means Harlan is nervous.
Marlowe's hand goes to his inside coat pocket for the snubnose. It's empty. He forgot to put it back.
Marlowe walks home through the harbor at night. The cranes are still lit up. The work never stops.
The crimson scarf. He remembers seeing it once before, in 1949, on someone else. A woman named Estelle.
Final beat: the tone should be resignation, not defeat. He'll go on. The city goes on. Nothing is solved and everyone knows it.
